Cloud-Native Banking & Transaction Engine

Distributed FinTech backend implementing ACID-compliant fund transfers, idempotency keys, JWT role-based security, and event-driven audit logging with Spring Boot and PostgreSQL.

Author: Rohit Sharma (Principal Systems Architect & Placement Mentor)
Reviewed by Ananya Verma
Updated: Sep 30, 2026

Problem Statement & Objectives

Financial systems cannot afford dirty reads, double-debit anomalies, or race conditions when concurrent requests attempt to withdraw from or transfer money between bank accounts simultaneously.

Real-World Context:Core banking engines, digital wallet platforms (like Paytm / PhonePe architectures), inter-bank settlement gateways, and neobank ledger platforms.

Key Project Objectives:

  • •Architect decoupled microservices for User Management, Account Balance Ledgers, and Transaction Auditing.
  • •Enforce strict transaction boundaries using pessimistic write locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) to prevent double-spending race conditions.
  • •Implement idempotency keys for all mutating transfer endpoints to ensure network retries never result in duplicate financial deductions.
  • •Secure all communication channels with stateless JWT authentication and role-based access control (RBAC).

System Architecture

The system utilizes an API Gateway routing traffic to three distinct Spring Boot services: Auth Service (JWT issuance), Account Service (balance management with pessimistic locking), and Transaction Ledger Service (immutable audit trail). Database transactions execute at `SERIALIZABLE` or `READ_COMMITTED` with row-level locking on balance modifications.

Database Design (Relational (PostgreSQL 16))

Strict 3NF normalized schema with foreign key constraints, check constraints ensuring balances never fall below zero, and B-Tree indexes on account numbers.

Table: usersPK: id (BIGSERIAL)

Customer and administrative profiles.

idusernameemailpassword_hashrolecreated_at
Table: accountsPK: account_number (VARCHAR 20)

Financial ledger accounts with balance check constraints.

account_numberuser_idcurrencybalance_centsstatusversion
Table: transactionsPK: id (UUID)

Immutable ledger entries recording fund transfers.

idsource_accountdestination_accountamount_centsidempotency_keytimestampstatus

Step-by-Step Implementation Guide

Step 1: Account Entity with Versioning & Balance Validation

Define the JPA Account entity with `@Entity`, currency formatting stored in smallest currency units (cents/paise) to eliminate floating-point rounding errors.

Account.java
@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts")
public class Account {
    @Id
    private String accountNumber;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private Long balanceCents;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    public void debit(Long amount) {
        if (this.balanceCents < amount) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException("Account has insufficient balance");
        }
        this.balanceCents -= amount;
    }

    public void credit(Long amount) {
        this.balanceCents += amount;
    }
}

Step 2: Atomic Transfer Service with Row Locking

Execute transfer inside `@Transactional` boundary, acquiring pessimistic write locks on both accounts ordered by account number to prevent database deadlocks.

TransferService.java
@Service
public class TransferService {
    @Autowired
    private AccountRepository accountRepository;

    @Transactional
    public TransactionResult executeTransfer(String fromAcc, String toAcc, Long amount) {
        // Order locks lexicographically to prevent deadlocks
        String firstLock = fromAcc.compareTo(toAcc) < 0 ? fromAcc : toAcc;
        String secondLock = fromAcc.compareTo(toAcc) < 0 ? toAcc : fromAcc;

        Account source = accountRepository.findByAccountNumberForUpdate(fromAcc);
        Account destination = accountRepository.findByAccountNumberForUpdate(toAcc);

        source.debit(amount);
        destination.credit(amount);

        return new TransactionResult(UUID.randomUUID(), "COMPLETED");
    }
}

Placement Viva & Technical Questions

Questions commonly asked by college examiners and product company interviewers regarding this project architecture.

Floating-point numbers in computer architectures cannot accurately represent decimal fractions in base-2 IEEE 754 standards (e.g., 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004). In banking systems, this causes roundoff discrepancy leaks over millions of transactions. We store monetary amounts in atomic integer units (cents/paise) or use Java's BigDecimal with explicit rounding modes.
